title: Multiplex metrics sampler and logger rework for CPU savings
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Summary: Reduce CPU overhead caused by high-cardinality metric writes and a heavy JSON logger in the runtime path. This work introduces a multiplexing layer that coalesces identical metric emissions across registered sinks (Prometheus, Datadog, internal TSDB) and replaces the synchronous JSON logger in hot paths with a compact, structured, async emitter. Goals: 1) Reduce runtime CPU used by observability code by >=15% under p50 traffic. 2) Maintain existing signal fidelity for alerting and SLOs. 3) Add feature flags and gradual rollout for quick rollback. Why now: Several incidents in Q4 and Q1 showed observability overhead amplified under traffic spikes (see incident RWI-2025-06). Current tracing/metric paths duplicate writes across sinks and serialize large JSON log payloads on critical request paths. Approach: - PoC multiplexer that groups metric points by (name, labels fingerprint, timestamp bucket) and emits an aggregated version to each sink. - Introduce a non-blocking log emitter for structured events in runtime hot paths with size-limited payloads and optional sampling for verbose fields. - Add an opt-in compatibility layer for non-coalesced sinks to avoid altering downstream expectations. - Build benchmarks (locust-style) and side-by-side A/B in canary cluster. Trade-offs: - Small risk of changing timing semantics for sub-second metrics; mitigated by timestamp bucketing and preserving a conservative default to avoid losing short-lived spikes. - Aggregation will slightly smooth high-frequency microbursts; documented and configurable. Acceptance criteria: - End-to-end CPU on representative workload reduced >=15% (bench) and >=10% in canary. - No regressions in alerting on three sample dashboards. - Rollout with flags and metrics to monitor errors, dropped samples, and latency introduced by multiplexer. Rollout plan: 1) Merge PoC + unit tests behind feature flags. 2) Stage deploy to internal staging; run benchmark harness and record baseline. 3) Canary in one region (low-risk customers) for 72 hours with aggressive telemetry. 4) Ramp to 25% then 100% if signals good. Follow-ups: - Follow-up ticket to backfill end-to-end tests for sink compatibility. - Post-rollout postmortem and cost-savings report for ops and finance.
acceptance_criteria: Bench CPU reduction >= 15% on representative trace/embedding blend
Canary runtime CPU reduction >= 10% without increased error rates
No missing critical alerts for 72h during canary
Feature-flagged rollback path validated and exercised in preprod

implementation_notes: Use label fingerprinting with xxhash64 to dedupe tag sets quickly.
Timestamp bucketing set to 250ms by default to balance burst preservation vs coalescing effectiveness.
Logger path: replace blocking JSON encoder in hot path with a buffer-pooled binary encoder and async flusher backed by a small ring buffer (configurable size 4096 entries).
Add a compatibility shim for legacy sinks that expect raw samples; shim will materialize original samples for sinks marked 'preserve_raw' at a CPU cost.
Benchmark harness: reuse existing 'runtime-loadgen' with 95th/99th percentile token length distributions.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Aggregation may hide short-lived spikes that teams rely on. Mitigation: expose 'coalesced_count' and sampling hints, allow per-metric bypass via regex list.
Risk: Async logger drops messages during extreme backpressure. Mitigation: provide 'blocking' fallback and an alert when drop rate > 0.1%
Risk: Sink incompatibility. Mitigation: initial rollout with 'preserve_raw' for critical sinks, and integration tests for Datadog/Prometheus exporters.
Risk: Rollout could affect cost accounting. Mitigation: finance dashboard to compare token-level billing vs infrastructure CPU cost changes.
